cards.front: What are the three stages in the life cycle of a Java program?
cards.extra: Source in a text editor → javac produces bytecode → the JVM turns bytecode into machine code the CPU runs.
cards.source: startertutorials.com — Life cycle of a Java program (https://www.startertutorials.com/corejava/life-cycle-java-program.html)

cards.front: What is the input and output of javac?
cards.extra: The bytecode is machine-independent — that is the whole point of the design. It is not binary the CPU can run directly.
cards.source: startertutorials.com — Life cycle of a Java program (https://www.startertutorials.com/corejava/life-cycle-java-program.html)

cards.front: What is the JVM's input and output?
cards.back: Input bytecode; output machine code for the local CPU
cards.extra: This is the step that makes Java portable: the same .class file runs anywhere a JVM exists.
cards.source: startertutorials.com — Life cycle of a Java program (https://www.startertutorials.com/corejava/life-cycle-java-program.html)

cards.back: It targets the JVM, not a CPU or operating system
cards.extra: Only the JVM is platform-specific. Write and compile once, run wherever a JVM is installed.
cards.source: startertutorials.com — Life cycle of a Java program (https://www.startertutorials.com/corejava/life-cycle-java-program.html)

cards.front: What does the file name have to do with the class name?
cards.back: The convention is ClassName.java; for a public class it is mandatory
cards.extra: A public class named Sample must live in Sample.java, or javac refuses to compile it. Non-public classes may share a file with the public one.
cards.source: startertutorials.com — Life cycle of a Java program (https://www.startertutorials.com/corejava/life-cycle-java-program.html)
